title: Brazil’s Lula says he now backs lowering age of criminal responsibility to 16
author: Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro
text:
Lula reverses position on age of responsibility for ‘heinous’ crimes in what many see as a desperate electoral gambit

Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva , has announced that he now supports lowering the age of criminal responsibility for “heinous” crimes from 18 to 16, reversing a longstanding policy in what is widely seen as a desperate electoral gambit.

The U-turn, which Lula announced during a Thursday night interview with TV Globo, comes with the presidential runoff in just over a week. The incumbent faces an uphill battle to overturn the first-round victory of his opponent, the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who remains slightly ahead at the polls.

Both the senator and his father, the former president, Jair Bolsonaro, have long supported lowering the age of criminal responsibility – they want it reduced to 14 rather than 16 – but Lula and his party have always opposed the change.

After repeated opinion polls, the latest of them this week, showed that 80% of the population supports lowering the age, Lula said: “My view, as a Brazilian citizen, is that for any and every heinous crime, I am in favour of lowering the age.”

He answered “yes” when the reporter asked whether he meant lowering it to 16.

The list of crimes classified as “heinous” under Brazilian law is extensive, ranging from murder and rape to the falsification of medicines and drug trafficking – the offence for which about a quarter of the 816,000 people serving prison sentences in Brazil were incarcerated.

Human rights organisations and security experts have long criticised proposals to lower the age of criminal responsibility, arguing that they do little to tackle violence while increasing recruitment into organised crime in Brazil’s overcrowded prisons.

On Thursday, before Lula’s interview, the proposal had been discussed in the senate. The Episcopal Conference of Brazil, a Catholic bishops’ organisation, had criticised it for “not addressing the causes of violence”, adding that placing young people “prematurely in the prison system tends to deepen cycles of violence and exclusion, undermining their rehabilitation”.

The columnist Josias de Souza wrote in his UOL column that, by reversing his longstanding position, Lula “decided to change himself. It was no ordinary transformation. On public security, Lula turned himself inside out. He began defending what he had always rejected.”

The incumbent has doubled down in recent days in an effort to overturn Bolsonaro’s 2.2 million-vote first-round lead by appealing to independents and undecided voters. He has secured congressional approval for a shorter working week – a proposal on which Bolsonaro himself U-turned and decided to support at the last minute, when it appeared ready to pass – and debt relief for microentrepreneurs, as well as promising free public transport on weekends.

title: Israeli settlers attack olive farmers and Washington Post journalist in West Bank
author: William Christou
text:
Settlers hurl rocks at Palestinians and beat photographer Heidi Levine as part of yearly attacks to disrupt harvest

Israeli settlers have attacked Palestinians across the occupied West Bank in a coordinated movement to disrupt the annual olive harvest, burning cars and trees and injuring Palestinians and a Washington Post photographer.

Masked settlers wielding clubs and other weapons attacked people attempting to harvest their olives in towns across the West Bank on Friday. At least six people were injured in the town of Abu Falah near Ramallah, the Palestinian Red Crescent Society said.

At least 80 settlers, some of whom were carrying firearms or clubs, gathered to stop Palestinians from harvesting their olives in Abu Falah, using slingshots to hurl rocks at the farmers in view of Israeli military vehicles. When some of the Palestinians then picked up rocks to defend themselves, the Israeli military fired teargas in their direction.

The Israeli Foreign Press Association said in a statement: “This is the latest in a long line of violent attacks by Israeli settlers against journalists and other civilians in the occupied West Bank. Yet our repeated calls for action to confront this lawlessness have been ignored by Israeli authorities.”

Among those injured was the Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine, who was beaten by settlers in an attack that lasted more than 10 minutes, according to witnesses. Settlers stole her passport, phone, wallet and equipment.

“I was attacked, pushed to the ground. Luckily, I had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn’t even be here, because they just kept kicking and kicking me,” Levine said from a hospital bed in Ramallah. She said the attack ended when her Palestinian colleagues intervened to save her.

In a statement, the Washington Post said Levine had been wearing visible markings clearly identifying her as a journalist.

There has been a surge of settler violence against Palestinians over the past month. Settlers have carried out at least 170 attacks since 27 September, around the start of the annual olive harvest, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli rights group.

Every year, settlers attack Palestinians trying to harvest their olives, but this year’s harvest has seen an uptick in violence as Israel’s elections approach at the end of October.

At least four Palestinians have been killed and more than 100 others have been injured over the past month, Palestinian authorities said. Thousands of trees have been damaged.

Israel imposed new rules on the olive harvest this year, barring Palestinians from harvesting their trees located in Area C – an area under the Israeli military’s control, which comprises most of the West Bank’s agricultural land.

The new orders prohibit Palestinians from entering about 8,800 hectares (21,800 acres) of agricultural land – a 30% increase from the year prior – without approval of the Israeli military. By contrast, the military gave Israeli citizens access to more land this year.

The rights group Peace Now says the military decreased the amount of land Israeli citizens were prohibited from entering from about 1,070 hectares in 2025 to 680 hectares in 2026, for the purpose of preventing settler violence.

The olive harvest is an economic lifeline for Palestinians and has grown in importance since Israel revoked work permits for many Palestinians in the West Bank after the Hamas-led attack on 7 October 2023.

Photos and videos showed large swathes of agricultural land with uprooted olive trees in Kufur Malek, outside Ramallah, where Israeli bulldozers had razed trees.

Settlers rarely face accountability for their violence, even when well documented. Rights groups say settlers enjoy the protection of the Israeli military, which intervenes only if Palestinians try to defend themselves.

The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has on occasion condemned the violence, which he says is due to just about 100 settlers, but he has taken few steps to stop settler violence.

Settlements have rapidly expanded across the West Bank under his rightwing government, leading to international condemnation. The UN and most countries judge settlements to be in violation of international law.

Friday’s attack in Abu Falah followed a similar attack hours earlier near the West Bank village of Turmus Ayya, where settlers burned three cars after attacking Palestinians harvesting olives.

Videos shared by the Israeli rights group B’tselem showed hundreds of bags of olives “violently” stolen by Israeli settlers from Palestinians and taken to Israeli olive presses.

Sarit Michaeli, an independent activist, said settlers were stealing Palestinians’ olive crop on a scale “never seen before in my 22-year history of working on this issue”.

A spokesperson for the US embassy in Jerusalem said it was aware of reports of the attack and declined to comment further due to privacy laws.

title: India’s Cockroach Janta party leader arrested amid crackdown on protests
author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Delhi
text:
Abhijeet Dipke was arrested before planned anti-government demonstrations in Delhi

The leader of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) youth movement, Abhijeet Dipke, was detained by police on Friday as authorities cracked down on fresh anti-government protests in the Indian capital.

Dipke was detained before a planned Friday evening demonstration he had called in central Delhi , urging supporters of the movement to come out and hold up the Indian flag.

The Cockroach movement initially emerged back in May as online satire, but has since grown into one of the most substantial challenges to the powerful Modi government over its 12-year rule.

Alongside student groups and opposition parties, its supporters have in the past month been out on the streets across India’s biggest cities calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing a revision of India’s electoral rolls that allegedly favours the ruling Narendra Modi government with the deletion of 130m names. The election commission and Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) deny the claims.

The authorities, particularly in Delhi, have met the recent protests with a draconian crackdown, including bans on public gatherings, the deployment of tens of thousands of police, and detentions of thousands last weekend.

Friday’s protest was called by Dipke after the arrest and jailing of two of his fellow CJP leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka. They were sentenced to five days in jail this week for jumping police barricades and holding a brief protest – including waving the Indian flag – at a site recently restricted by police for demonstrations in Delhi.

At a press conference on Thursday, Dipke condemned the “repressive” attempts to silence the CJP movement and called on supporters to come out and show Narendra Modi “that we are not afraid”. He added: “If waving the Indian national flag lands you in jail, we are ready.”

Delhi police had once again taken extreme measures to try to prevent Friday’s demonstration, due to be held at a park in a busy commercial centre in the heart of Delhi, from going ahead. Police were deployed en masse to the area and a police notice was sent to Dipke instructing him to call off the protest. The Delhi local authority also shut down the park where the protest was due to take place.

When Dipke refused to call it off, police detained him en route, just as people began to assemble for the protest. In videos captured of his arrest, the CJP leader was seen holding an Indian flag aloft and saying: “I have not broken any law right now … how can you detain me?” as he was led away by dozens of police officers.

In a post after his detention, the CJP posted on social media: “This government is so scared of the youth waving national flag.”

Neha Bora, a student leader who has become a figurehead of the protests, was also detained on Friday as she began a march in the centre of the capital.

Despite Dipke’s detention, about 2,000 protesters still gathered and unfurled flags at the protest around Delhi’s Connaught Place. Among them was 23-year-old Sanna, who said the brutal police crackdown on peaceful protests over recent weeks demonstrated that India was “on a pathway to dictatorship under the Modi government”.

“We are only out here to peacefully hold up the Indian flag and they treat us as if we are criminals, not citizens exercising our democratic rights,” she said. “Gyanesh Kumar must resign, and no matter what the police do, detaining us or crushing our skulls, we still won’t stop protesting until he is gone.”

Smaller protests also took place in Mumbai, Bengaluru and Patna on Friday.

The BJP has claimed that the Cockroach movement and the political opposition alliance have been holding protests to cause “anarchy” in the country. “Their sole intention is to stage a coup in the country,” said the BJP’s national spokesperson, Sambit Patra.

The authorities have also gone to unusual lengths to punish figures who have been seen at the recent protests calling for Kumar’s resignation.

In Mumbai, the Bollywood actor Imran Khan was given a notice to leave the country after he was detained by police while attending a demonstration last weekend. Khan, who holds a US passport, was told to leave the country by the end of the month, an order he is now challenging in the courts.

title: Extreme heatwaves in Europe not changing Britons’ holiday plans, say travel bosses
author: Gwyn Topham Transport correspondent
text:
Hot summer getaways are still popular – but tourism industry fears impact of rising jet fuel costs and squeezed household incomes

After a year marked by extreme heat and war sending fuel prices skywards, British travel executives hoped for solace in Madeira’s benign subtropical climate, separated by hundreds of miles of blue sea from the overtourism protests and six-hour EU-entry queues seen on the Portuguese mainland.

As bosses admitted, holidays will be ever less affordable, AI is coming for their jobs, and the visitable world is shrinking – not least those parts where tourists remain welcome.

Some of the bigger anxieties in spring , such as widespread border chaos and planes running out of fuel, have not come to pass; others now appear chronic issues. New supplies of jet fuel, a major concern after the US first attacked Iran in February, have been established – but the cost is staying far higher for longer than most expected.

“Fuel is a huge part of any holiday and people are going to have to reckon with the cost,” said Neil Swanson, Tui UK & Ireland managing director, among the attendees at the Abta convention.

Tui and airlines such as easyJet and Ryanair escaped the worst immediate impact by having secured much of their 2026 fuel supply at a fixed price. But the latter airlines are now slashing capacity for winter.

“It’s not great for consumers, who are going to have to pay a lot more for their holidays. But airlines are going to be less and less hedged and prices are going to go up,” Swanson added.

The oil price impact goes beyond jet fuel, said Mark Tanzer, the chief executive of Abta: “The bigger worry is the squeeze on household incomes that’s going to come through their domestic costs. It will be a much tighter market.”

Perhaps surprisingly, numbers have held up – but customers have been leaving it ever later to book, he said, whether in search of a deal or because of uncertainty from disruption, war or weather.

Despite the intense heat, mass travel firms are clear that the template has not changed: most customers still want a hot holiday, in summer, on the beach.

Garry Wilson, the chief executive of easyJet Holidays, said: “Will there be long-term effects on demand? Perhaps. But in the short-term, no, we don’t see it.”

Growing “shoulder season” travel outside the school holidays for those who can, including city breaks, are driven by price more than climate, several people suggest. And talk of “coolcations” or people turning towards northern climes cuts little ice here. “We’re not seeing any of that,” said Swanson. “Nothing’s changed, the destinations are the same.”

When Tunisia was forecast a 10-day stretch of 45C temperatures this summer, Tui offered customers the chance to switch their holiday elsewhere. Swanson said: “We didn’t get the interest and take-up. People were expecting it to be hot and were happy to go there, and we’re not seeing any change in demand. Brits like a warm holiday – if it’s got a pool and air-conditioning, that works for them.”

Neither does Wilson see many heading north. Citing easyJet destinations such as Tromsø in Norway or Malmö in Sweden, he said: “They’re all very nice to launch, but we send more customers to Majorca in a week than those in a year.”

Outbound holidays prospered in the heatwave, he suggested. “People thought: ‘You know what, we maybe don’t need to go away.’ But it became apparent that the UK doesn’t have the infrastructure to cope … people actually were going abroad to escape the heat in the UK.”

For now, the big firms see little change in destinations, Swanson said, but added: “We’ll keep it under review. Who knows where the temperature’s going to go in the next few years?”

More people could get priced out. At last year’s convention, the Spanish tourist board started pushing its cooler northern destinations; but, said Tanzer, “I’m not sure the north has 100m beds” to accommodate the visitors who predominantly go to Spain’s south, east and islands.

He added: “Certain types of holiday could become more expensive just because there’s limited availability. If the snow is higher up the mountain, there’s going to be fewer skiing holidays and the price is going to go up – there’s little room at the top.”

Tui has not been immune. Its river cruises in Europe were marooned when the Danube’s water levels dipped last month to the point where some passengers spent most of their return Austro-Hungarian cruise on a boat-replacement bus.

Katy Berzins, the head of river cruises at Tui, said: “Every year has highs and lows and it’s part of river cruising, rivers are changeable.” But 2026, she said, was “unprecedented”.

The division is expanding nonetheless. Two new ships are joining its fleet – initially destined for the Seine and the Douro – that are built with lower draught levels (the vessel’s vertical depth below the surface), meaning they are able to keep sailing in shallower rivers.

Others are seeing faster change. James Thornton, the chief executive of Intrepid Travel, said the firm no longer sold active travel group tours in southern Europe in the summer; few had wanted to trek or cycle in that level of heat.

Last year, Thornton said, there were 185 different extreme weather-related incidents that affected Intrepid holidaymakers around the world. “When we first started, there would be a handful.”

Intrepid has long wrestled with its own impact on climate: for years, before offsetting fell into disrepute, it paid millions to offset its emissions. That did not cover the biggest factor, the flights taken by its customers to reach Intrepid tours – not entirely dissimilar from how an airport might declare itself net zero. Instead now the firm has a decarbonisation fund for local projects: “Ultimately you can’t have sustainable travel, you can only limit the impact,” Thornton said.…

title: ‘Tough to watch, impossible to ignore’: reviewers on NAZA documentary
author: Sammy Gecsoyler
text:
Film interviewing military insiders about mass killing of civilians in Gaza wins widespread praise around the world

Critics around the world have hailed the award-winning documentary NAZA as a “brilliant and harrowing” film that is “impossible to ignore”.

NAZA, which is produced by the Guardian and details Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza, was released in UK cinemas this week and will be shown in more than 50 countries. As well as its global cinema releases, NAZA will be available free on the Guardian’s website from late November.

The investigative documentary, which contains 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders speaking anonymously on the rooftops of Tel Aviv at night, has received widespread praise.

In a five-star review, the Financial Times’s Danny Leigh says that as a piece of cinema, “journalism and film-making brilliantly entwine”. The Times calls the film “hugely provocative and a disturbing account” of Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza, and the Irish Times brands NAZA an “essential record of engineered nightmare”. In a four-star review, the Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw says the “ anguish of Gaza is brought into pin-sharp focus ”.

British Vogue calls NAZA a “brilliant and harrowing film” that outlines the “restrained, meticulous, bone-chilling depiction of the progressive erasure of Gaza”. The magazine says the film “feels destined to become an enduring historical document, one which will and should be seen by generations to come”.

Time Out magazine says NAZA “puts together a restrained, intelligent, articulate, precise and utterly damning case against Israel’s actions in Gaza and their ongoing actions through the region. As a work of cinema, it is exemplary. As a work of journalism, it is inarguable. As a document, it is an indictment.”

The New York Times makes the film a “critic’s choice” and calls NAZA a “haunting” documentary that is “tough to watch, and impossible to ignore”. The Los Angeles Times says NAZA is a “stone-cold frightening” film that “burns the conscience”. And in New York magazine, it is described as “one of the most important films of our time”.

The Hollywood Reporter praises NAZA as a “sober and thoroughly documented bombshell of an exposé” that “leaves one with a deadening feeling, as if humanity may have lost all hope”. The Toronto Star says “NAZA is heartbreaking but essential viewing, questioning the systems that cause and quantify civilian death in modern warfare”.

The Spanish outlet El Mundo hailed NAZA as “the film of our time, a superb, electrifying, and devastating documentary about the systematic model of annihilation of the Palestinian people” that ultimately “points the finger at us. At night, in silence.”

The French newspaper Le Monde says the film “has the effect of an uppercut that leaves the viewer stunned”, while the Danish culture magazine Soundvenue calls NAZA a “soul-crushing testimony to the genocide in Gaza” that is an “example of how the world increasingly seems like a dystopia”.

The United Arab Emirates’ state-owned newspaper the National calls NAZA a “sickeningly tough film to watch”, and an editorial in the Israeli-outlet Haaretz says the film is “trying to force Israelis to confront what they already know: that Israel’s conduct of the war in Gaza has left a black stain”.

When the film opened in Italy last month, it topped the charts . The Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera says NAZA lasts “only 80 minutes, but no more is needed: the ‘scientific’ coldness with which the interviewees reconstruct how they are destroying Gaza is something unforgettable”.

The film contains 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders who detail how an AI-assisted apparatus of mass surveillance was activated during the Gaza war, revealing the systems that were used to target Hamas operatives in the knowledge that large numbers of Palestinian civilians would also die.

Various organisations, including the UN, Amnesty International, B’Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights, the latter two of which are Israeli-based, have said Israel is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

The film premiered at the Venice film festival, where it was received a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record. The documentary went on to win the special jury prize .

title: Meta may use sweeping new commercial TOS to avoid millions in AI licensing fees
author: Ashley Belanger
text:
Legal experts are sounding alarms that Meta will soon update its commercial terms to require business accounts to allow Meta to train AI on their linked website content, not just their social media posts.

Kicking in on October 30, the TOS update won’t allow businesses to opt out, instead suggesting that businesses stop using Meta services if they won’t agree to let Meta bots freely crawl their linked content.

As Nieman Lab reported Thursday, this will affect all business accounts but is particularly shocking for news publishers who could perhaps charge Meta millions in licensing fees to continually access their articles for AI training. Currently news organizations are fighting a battle with OpenAI over whether such training without licensing is fair use, and Meta's terms seemingly risk granting it sweeping permissions, no matter which way the court leans.

Richard Carapaz Breaks Contract with EF Education-EasyPost to Join NSN in Transfer Stunner
author: Jim Cotton
text:
Richard Carapaz has split from EF Education-EasyPost to join NSN Cycling Team on a three-year deal that will see him toward retirement.

The bombshell transfer was confirmed Friday afternoon after a wave of speculation following recent reports by Wielerflits .

The 33-year-old had an ongoing contract with the American EF Education-EasyPost team and had enjoyed a wildly successful 2026 season.

He finished top-10 at both the Tour de France and Vuelta a España, and claimed the Tour de France KoM jersey for a second time.

According to Wielerflits , EF Education-EasyPost is suffering a budget pinch going into 2027. The Ecuadorian would have been one of the highest-paid riders on the roster of Jonathan Vaughters’ team.

Carapaz’s exit will be hard felt at EF. He’s been the center of the squad’s ambitions for the past four seasons.

Beyond that, the U.S. team was already reeling from a rider exodus. Five others, including classics talent Kasper Asgreen, have recently confirmed they’re leaving this winter. Asgreen also joins NSN Cycling Team in 2027.

Meanwhile, EF Education-EasyPost has confirmed only one incoming transfer for 2027. Young American Gavin Sherry steps up from the EF-Aevolo devo team.

“Gracias, Richie. Por todo,” EF wrote in a montage video of Carapaz’s greatest hits it posted to Instagram .

NSN Cycling Team heralded Carapaz’s arrival Friday as “a major statement that will strengthen the roster and the team’s grand tour and stage race ambitions.”

The former Giro d’Italia winner and Olympic champion will join Santiago Buitrago and Lennert Van Eetvelt in a new climbing division of the Swiss-registered squad.

Having only formed out of the ashes of Israel Premier-Tech at the start of 2026, NSN was focused on sprints with Biniam Girmay and Ethan Vernon in its debut season.

“For me, it’s a tremendous opportunity as a rider to be part of this project and, above all, to be one of the team’s leaders,” Carapaz said Friday.

“I find the NSN project really interesting. After our first conversations, I was convinced this would be the right place for me. I’m a rider who has achieved great results throughout my career, many of which were in the grand tours, and that fits very well with what NSN was looking for,” Carapaz continued.

“The team has big ambitions to keep growing and already in my conversations with the performance team, it was clear we share the same desire to keep improving and achieve big things together.”

title: How Horner, Brown and Wolff made their fortunes from F1
author: Darren Cox
text:
Christian Horner, Zak Brown and Toto Wolff have been three of the most influential team bosses during Formula 1's extraordinary growth over the past decade.

All three have been very well rewarded for it. But the latest set of F1 team accounts filed in the UK reveal something more interesting than simply how much each has made.

They show three very different ways of sharing in the value that has been created as F1 teams have gone from businesses that often needed wealthy owners to keep funding them to scarce sporting assets now worth billions.

Horner was ultimately a very highly paid employee at Red Bull. Brown has participated in McLaren's growth through a long-term incentive scheme. Wolff owns a significant part of the Mercedes team he runs.

The difference between the three helps explain why ownership now appears to be so important to Horner as he considers what he does next.

Red Bull Technology's 2025 accounts disclose £66.988million in compensation for loss of office for its highest-paid director, understood to be Horner, alongside £9.029m in remuneration.

That puts his disclosed package for the year at around £76m.

Some reports have put the compensation above £100m by adding a separate £33.494m figure contained in Red Bull Racing's accounts. But Red Bull Technology explicitly states that its £66.988m disclosure is for the group, which includes Red Bull Racing. The £33.494m should therefore not be added again.

Even £76m is an extraordinary sum.

But perhaps the most interesting thing about Horner's 20 years at Red Bull isn't what he made. It's what he didn't have: ownership.

That should not be confused with Horner having made a bad deal when he joined Red Bull. Quite the opposite.

At the end of 2004 he was 31, had built a successful Formula 3000 team in Arden, and was trying to find a way into F1. He had looked at buying Jordan but simply didn't have the hundreds of millions required to make the step independently.

Then Dietrich Mateschitz bought Jaguar and turned it into Red Bull Racing.

Horner later recalled being summoned to Salzburg and Mateschitz telling him he had big ambitions for the team and was "willing to take a chance" on him. Horner said he was only 31 and "didn't have to think about it for too long".

And the deal itself wasn't bad either. Horner has since recalled that Mateschitz told him he wouldn't be paid a huge salary but would receive a healthy bonus for every point Red Bull scored. Jaguar had managed nine points the previous season. Red Bull scored 34 in its first.

For a 31-year-old team owner trying to find his way into F1, it was an extraordinary opportunity.

Horner helped turn Red Bull Racing from the remains of Jaguar into one of F1's most successful teams, winning six constructors' championships and eight drivers' titles.

But however well he was rewarded, Horner remained an employee of a business owned by somebody else.

Brown's situation at McLaren is different.

McLaren Racing's accounts show its highest-paid director received £81.897m in 2025, comprising £8.215m in remuneration and £73.682m relating to its long-term incentive scheme. Brown has been identified as that director in reporting of the accounts.

The bulk of the package resulted from an incentive scheme connected to the enormous increase in the value of McLaren Racing.

The turnaround has been remarkable. McLaren was in serious financial trouble during the pandemic and brought outside investment into its racing operation. Five years later, the transaction that consolidated the ownership of McLaren Racing valued the business at around £3.5billion.

Brown therefore had a substantial participation in the increase in McLaren Racing's value through his incentive arrangements, allowing him to share in the upside as the business was transformed.

The comparison with Horner is striking. Both received packages of around £80m in 2025, but they got there in completely different ways.

Horner's was dominated by the compensation he received for leaving the business he had spent two decades building. Brown's was dominated by an incentive designed to give him a share of the value created as McLaren Racing grew.

Wolff's position is different again. Mercedes' accounts disclose £9.528m of total directors' remuneration in 2025, although they don't tell us how much of that was Wolff's individually.

His executive pay is, in any case, almost incidental to the important number. Because Wolff owns the asset.

When INEOS bought into Mercedes' F1 operation , the team was divided equally between Mercedes-Benz, INEOS and Wolff's investment vehicle. Wolff therefore had a one-third economic interest in Mercedes F1 while also serving as its team principal and CEO.

That also allows him to participate in the profits distributed by the business. Mercedes paid £125m in dividends in 2025, meaning a one-third shareholder would have an economic interest in roughly £42m of that if the distribution was made pro rata. That money would, of course, flow through the relevant ownership structures rather than simply appearing as part of Wolff's salary.

But last year provided a much bigger indication of what his original investment has become worth.

Mercedes confirmed the structure but did not disclose the price. The transaction was reported as valuing Mercedes F1 at around $6bn, with Wolff receiving approximately $300m for the stake he sold.

And he only sold 15% of his holding.

Wolff retained the remaining 85%, equivalent to approximately 28.3% of Mercedes F1. At the same $6bn valuation, that stake would be worth around $1.7bn.

That isn't $1.7bn sitting in Wolff's bank account. It is the implied value of a shareholding based on the valuation attached to a minority transaction.

But it shows the enormous difference between being paid to create value and owning the value you create.

Horner spent more than two decades building Red Bull Racing and was extremely well rewarded as an employee, including a remarkable payment when that relationship ended.

Brown helped take McLaren Racing from the edge of a financial crisis to a business valued at around £3.5bn, with an incentive structure that allowed him to participate directly in that increase in value.

Wolff did something different. He bought into the business he was running.

As the value of F1 teams has exploded, that has proved to be the ultimate deal.

Which brings us back to Horner.

Since leaving Red Bull, he has become increasingly clear about wanting something different from the next stage of his career.

His language now is particularly interesting when compared with the 31-year-old who described the original Red Bull opportunity as a "no-brainer".

"I've been a hired hand," Horner said recently. "I did 21 years sitting on the pitwall. I don't need to go back to that."

His preference now is to return as "a partner, rather than just a hired hand".

It isn't difficult to understand why.

The original Red Bull deal was a fantastic one for Horner in 2005. What changed over the following 21 years was F1 itself, and particularly the value of its teams.

F1 teams were once sporting operations that routinely consumed their owners' money. Today, the best of them are global sports businesses worth billions.

If Horner is going to spend the next decade helping to build another one, you can see why this time he appears determined to own a piece of it.

title: Carrick brushes off Martínez’s failure to apologise publicly to United director Wilcox
author: Jamie Jackson
text:
Manchester United coach accepts defender’s apology

‘He’s realised he’s made a mistake and that’s enough’

Michael Carrick brushed off Lisandro Martínez’s failure to offer Jason Wilcox a public apology after the defender criticised Manchester United’s director of football in the wake of Tuesday’s defeat at Atlético Madrid .

Martínez referred directly to Wilcox after the 2-0 Champions League loss, saying: “I expect more from our technical director.”

On Thursday Martínez issued an apology that did not mention Wilcox or withdraw the essence of his outburst: the need for more squad investment. “The frustration of the defeat led me to express how I felt at a time and place that perhaps were not the right ones, and for that I want to apologise,” he said.

Carrick was asked whether he respected Martínez for not saying sorry to Wilcox. “He’s released his statement, he’s realised he’s made a mistake and that’s enough for all of us to move on with,” United’s manager said.

Carrick was pressed on whether it would have been better if Martínez had apologised to Wilcox and for his wider comments about investment, rather than just saying sorry for the timing and location of his interview. “From our point of view, the acknowledgment of what’s been done has certainly been enough, we’ve moved on and we’re definitely not looking back at it now,” he replied.

Carrick said Martínez was available for Sunday’s trip to Leeds, where Manchester United go having taken only six points from their opening six league games. They were knocked out of the Carabao Cup by Brighton last month and have one win and a defeat in the Champions League. Poor form has increased the pressure on Carrick, who was asked whether Martínez’s comments were an unwanted distraction that had annoyed him.

“No, I understand emotion at times,” he said. “We ask for passion, we ask for emotion, we ask for fire and we ask for players to care. There’s a way of doing that, and that’s already been acknowledged, but we need to carry that intensity and that willingness and that togetherness and that spirit. As a group, we need to use it, and we’ve got to use it in the right way.”

Wayne Rooney, United’s record goalscorer, claimed Martínez’s comments “will rip the dressing room apart”. It was put to Carrick that they may have an opposite, unifying effect.

“There’s a lot of things that can affect the group in all sorts of different ways,” said Carrick, who went on to highlight his players’ reaction to conceding inside a minute at Atlético. “It’s one of the toughest places to play in the Champions League, so to go a goal down so early, and the way we responded shows an underlying belief and spirit and a togetherness,” he said.

He indicated that events on and off the pitch this week had brought the squad together. “Certain situations can galvanise the group, and it’s certainly galvanised the group as this week’s progressed. The boys are in a really good place right now.”

Carrick was asked why anyone outside the club, including former players such as Rooney who have criticised Martínez, should believe there is unity. “There’s a lot of people that say a lot of things, and ex-pros or not ex-pros, it doesn’t necessarily mean you understand what’s going on here,” he said. “I’m telling you the truth. The squad today [Friday] was in a fantastic place, better than I’ve seen it for a while.”

Carrick said Luke Shaw and Kobbie Mainoo faced fitness tests.

title: UK risks losing key role in European space industry over satellite contract, says Airbus boss
author: Jasper Jolly
text:
Guillaume Faury writes to Andy Burnham warning him against choosing US firm Lockheed Martin to build Skynet satellites

The boss of Airbus has told Andy Burnham that choosing its US rival Lockheed Martin to manufacture military satellites could cost the UK a key role in the European space industry, intensifying a last-minute lobbying effort for the £2.4bn contract.

It is understood that Guillaume Faury, the chief executive of France-headquartered Airbus, has written to the prime minister suggesting that the choice of provider of the Skynet system could have effects for decades to come on the UK’s strength in military satellites in Europe, in an effort to tip the contract away from its US rival.

Yet politicians in north-east England have lobbied in favour of the Lockheed Martin bid, which would include a new factory in Durham.

The military satellites under the Skynet 6 contract will carry the British armed forces’ most sensitive communications up to 2042, replacing the Skynet 5 system operated by Airbus .

The delayed decision on which company will manufacture the UK’s sovereign satellites comes at a sensitive moment, after Ukraine complained that its access to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite network was restricted , apparently at the behest of the US government.

Several sources said they believed no final decision on the contract had been made. However, some said they believed that Lockheed Martin’s bid was preferred by the Ministry of Defence . The final decision will rest with Burnham and the chancellor, John Healey.

It is thought that Faury’s letter warned of longer-term consequences for the UK’s role in the European space sector if Airbus were to lose out. Senior industry figures have previously claimed that Airbus’s UK satellite operations would not be viable without the next Skynet contract, meaning the company might close its sites at Stevenage and Portsmouth, which employ 600 people.

The manufacturers Airbus, Thales and Leonardo are working on a long-awaited merger between their space subsidiaries, known as Project Bromo, in an effort to build a single European champion with the scale to rival the leading US companies.

Faury is understood to have warned that if its British operation were no longer viable it could mean the UK missing out on the chance to be the European hub for military satellite communications once the merger was complete.

Lockheed Martin is one of the US’s largest defence “prime” contractors, but it says its UK subsidiary will have full control over the satellites eventually built in the UK. People close to Lockheed Martin have strongly denied that the US government would have control over the satellites.

A Lockheed Martin spokesperson said the company was “unable to comment on the ongoing procurement process”, but added: “Lockheed Martin UK, a British company, will establish facilities to develop an ecosystem alongside our regional partners in the north-east of England to provide the UK with a sovereign space capability. It will create jobs, supply chain opportunities and the potential for exports. It will have a UK design authority and a UK chief engineer.”

Luke Akehurst, the Labour MP for North Durham, said Lockheed’s bid would mean a “state-of-the-art new manufacturing facility” in the region. “This represents a massive investment in the reindustrialisation of the north-east of England, building on our region’s proud heritage of advanced manufacturing.”

The personal intervention from Faury, one of the most powerful executives in Europe, is a sign of the importance of the contract to Airbus, which is headquartered in Toulouse.

A decision had been expected in the summer but it has been delayed in part by the arrival of Burnham in office.

Unite, one of the Labour party’s biggest union backers, had warned against “handing the British space industry over to the Americans” at a time when there are increased questions over whether the UK can rely on the US government.

Burnham will also have to consider the two bids on their financial terms and the capabilities the two companies can offer.

A government document for a related system said satellites had to deal with the “proliferation of counterspace capabilities to disrupt, deny, degrade or destroy space-based enablers”. It highlighted radio jamming, hacking and direct physical attacks on the satellites as possible concerns.

The first Skynet satellite was launched in 1969, well before the use of the name for a hostile artificial intelligence in the 1984 film The Terminator .

Kim McGuinness, the mayor for north-east England, said: “Bringing satellite manufacturing to the north-east is a huge opportunity to build on what we have already achieved, including the close ties we have forged between our world-class universities and industry. If secured, this investment would be a gamechanger for the space and security sector, bringing £100m of investment and creating 500 high-skilled jobs as well as a much greater impact through the supply chain.”

title: Richard Carapaz breaks EF Education-EasyPost contract to sign for NSN
author: James Moultrie
text:
Richard Carapaz has broken his contract with EF Education-EasyPost early to join NSN Cycling Team on a three-year deal starting in 2027, it was confirmed on Friday. The 33-year-old Ecuadorian was due to remain on the US team until the end of 2027, but will instead ply his trade at the Swiss-registered squad, bringing "world-class climbing ability, experience, and leadership to the team."

Announced via a social media video with NSN co-founder and Spanish football icon Andres Iniesta, Carapaz is their seventh confirmed new signing for next season. He raced in the pink of EF for four successful seasons, with the US team posting a video of his recent highlights and behind-the-scenes moments with the caption "Gracias, Richie. Por todo."

A former Giro d'Italia winner, Olympic champion, three-time Tour de France stage winner, and winner of multiple Grand Tour King of the Mountains jerseys, Carapaz arrives as a true GC leader for NSN, finishing fourth at the Vuelta a España and eighth overall at the Tour just this past year. "For me, it’s a tremendous opportunity as a rider to be part of this project and, above all, to be one of the team’s leaders," said Carapaz.

"I’m simply very excited. I’m really looking forward to it, and to be honest, this reminds me a lot of when I signed my first professional contract, when I was incredibly excited about being in the WorldTour. I still have the same motivation as I did that day and that’s really an incredible feeling.

"I find the NSN project really interesting and after our first conversations, I was convinced this would be the right place for me. I’m a rider who has achieved great results throughout my career, many of which were in the Grand Tours, and that fits very well with what NSN was looking for.

"The team has big ambitions to keep growing and already in my conversations with the performance team, it was clear we share the same desire to keep improving and achieve big things together. I think the team has a lot of potential to develop and I’m excited to be part of that in the next three years." Carapaz's total haul of UCI points in 2026 was more than double that of NSN's top -ranked rider,

Biniam Girmay, so even into his 30s, he is still among the very best riders in the world and will lead their Grand Tour GC ambitions in the coming three years. "Signing Richard Carapaz is a significant moment for our team and an important milestone in the development of our sporting project," said General Manager Kjell Carlström.

"Richard is a proven champion. His achievements speak for themselves, but what makes him particularly special is his mentality. Richard is known for his grit and determination, and we saw this shine through in 2026 with his two Tour de France stage wins and the polka dot jersey, followed by an impressive podium a week later in San Sebastián.

"Richard is one of those riders whose passion for cycling is so evident and we believe he still has some of his best performances ahead of him. His experience and leadership will be extremely valuable, not only in helping us achieve our sporting objectives but also in developing the next generation of talent within the team. Richard is someone our young riders can look up to, and I have no doubt he will fit in perfectly in our team culture. We’re excited for Richard’s next chapter at NSN Cycling Team." Carapaz joins Santiago Buitrago, Lennert Van Eetvelt, Kasper Asgreen, Artem Shmidt and Cedric Beullens as new arrivals for 2027 at NSN. He's also the sixth confirmed departure for

EF Education-EasyPost at the end of the 2026 season.

title: Eneco Tour: Mick van Dijke nets maiden pro win as Victor Campenaerts moves into race lead on breathless stage 3
author: James Moultrie
text:
After a breathless day of racing, with groups split all over the road, Mick van Dijke (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) took the first professional win of his career from the breakaway on stage 3 of the Eneco Tour in Watersley.

The Dutch rider won ahead of new race leader Victor Campenaerts (Visma-Lease a Bike), after the pair bridged across to the original break in the last 33km, before getting away as the lead duo in the last 18km, and battling out the uphill sprint for the win.

Jonas Rutsch (Lotto Intermarché) and Pierre Thierry (TotalEnergies) survived from the early break to finish third and fourth, with Wessel Mouris (Unibet Rose Rockets) not far behind and jumping up to second overall as a result of his efforts.

Pre-stage race leader Jakob Söderqvist (Lidl-Trek) tried valiantly to defend the orange jersey, but dropped several times as racing heated up over the undulating Watersley circuit, eventually losing more than a minute and a half and the jersey.

Campenaerts now leads overall by 15 seconds from Mouris, with Finn Fisher-Black (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) sat third overall on a 30-second deficit. The orange jersey will be decided this weekend over two punchy stages to the Col du VAM and Arnhem.

"It's the first one. Finally, I'm chasing it already for five and a half years, so I'm super happy," said Van Dijke, then confirming that it was no gift from Campenaerts in the finale, but a result of one rider going for GC and the other the stage win.

"I don't know his name, but the French guy [Thierry] was not pulling anymore, and I said to Campy, 'If he doesn't pull, I won't pull'; then he attacked, and I had to go a little bit deep to catch him, but I managed to."

"We are big friends; Campy was riding for GC, so I was not allowed to pull. I told him that, and if I helped him a little bit, he did most of the work. Then in the end, he went full, and I also went full."

As a tough 110.5km route from Sittard to Watersley welcomed the remaining riders on race day four at the Eneco Tour, a four-rider break found themselves up the road after two laps of the circuit: Rutsch, Thierry, Jesse Kramer (BEAT CC p/b Saxo), and Rick Ottema (EEW-VDK Cyclingteam)

With 33km to go, four became seven as Hartthijs de Vries (Unibet Rose Rockets), Van Dijke, and Campenaerts attacked across the gap, with the latter's presence – having started the day just 29 seconds down on Söderqvist – forcing Lidl-Trek to chase in the peloton with two reps of the four hills still to come.

With 30km to go, Soudal-QuickStep started to accelerate, first with Tim Merlier, who was setting up an attack for Pepijn Reinderink. Quickly, Söderqvist found himself going backwards and struggling, but the riders at the front of the peloton began to mark each other as no one was able to get away.

The break started to fracture with the peloton breathing down their necks on the fourth and penultimate time up the Windraak, but the five who remained in front maintained their lead of just under 25 seconds heading into the last lap.

As Söderqvist was fully dropped in the last 20km, struggling to hold the wheels, Campenaerts started making his bid for the overall lead in front, taking the maximum six bonus seconds at the Red Bull KM and then attacking with 18km to go from the break.

Van Dijke was able to go with the Belgian, making it a leading duo in front of the first chase group containing fourth-place on GC Mouris, 21 seconds back, a second group containing Fisher-Black at 43 seconds back, and the peloton containing Söderqvist back at 1:01 heading into the final 10km.

With racing split all over the road, Fisher-Black launched an attack into the last 5.5km, but he was followed by Menno Huising (Visma-Lease a Bike) and the rest of the chasing group he was already in. Soon after, the Kiwi moved across the road and caused Huising – who was looking back at the group – to crash out of the chase.

They made no real impression on the leading duo, though; he entered the final kilometre after Campenaerts had done the lion's share of the work. Van Dijke won the uphill sprint for his maiden success, with the rest of the GC hopefuls coming home behind new orange jersey Campenaerts in dribs and drabs.

title: Polymarket saw $600 million in election trades after the elections were over
author: Kate Knibbs, wired.com
text:
Prediction market boosters often tout the platforms as barometers of public opinion, or even “truth machines” offering a clearer picture of where things are headed than polling or other data. In 2024, for example, Kalshi beat many pollsters in forecasting the outcome of the US presidential race. But their trading activity can also tell more perplexing stories.

Two global election markets on Polymarket’s offshore platform , for instance, generated over $600 million in trading volume, far more than most political markets typically attract. Most of the activity took place buying and selling contracts tied to long-shot candidates who ultimately did not win.

This summer, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s Prosperity Party cruised to victory in federal elections, winning 438 parliamentary seats and paving the way for him to serve another five-year term. The closest competitor won 13 seats. On prediction markets, trading volume—the total value of contracts bought and sold—typically tracks roughly with the odds of a given outcome; frontrunners attract far more volume than long shots. But in this case, the trading patterns deviated sharply from the norm. Just $173,000 was wagered on Ahmed winning, compared to more than $41 million traded on his chief of staff, Shimelis Abdisa, becoming the country’s next leader. Altogether, the volume traded added up to over $285 million, nearly all on losing candidates.

title: Tesla turns to 50-year-old stunt technology as it tries to Roadster again
author: Jonathan M. Gitlin
text:
The new Roadster, we’re told, will be unlike anything else, although the angular, wedge-shaped styling owes more than a little to Giorgetto Giugiaro’s original Lotus Esprit—Musk is known to own a James Bond prop car—as well as the more recent Lamborghini Gallardo. At the rear are four giant exhaust pipes; these do not signal Tesla’s sudden embrace of hydrocarbons beyond those emitted by private aviation.

Rather, it’s where 100,000 psi jets of compressed nitrogen shoot out. It’s early in the morning and the Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Statutes are dense reading, so I am yet to find the section where it explains how and when it’s legal to use such a thing on the road.

title: Super Scam Me documentary shows what it takes to catch a romance scammer
author: Ashley Belanger
text:
If you got a DM from an unverified Jon Bon Jovi account after commenting on one of his official Instagram posts, what would it take to make you believe it was really the rock star hoping to connect? And at what point when he starts asking you to send money—like lose-your-house kind of money—would you snap out of the fantasy and stop draining your bank account?

In a documentary premiering Saturday——investigative journalist Mariana van Zeller goes deep into this toxic love-bombing terrain. In a clip that Ars is exclusively debuting below, you can see how van Zeller worked with an ethical hacker, Arman the Cyber, to use a fake bitcoin receipt and bait the fake Bon Jovi, giving the victim some much-needed closure.

Sneak peek at National Geographic's .

Scamming a romance scammer

Broadcasting on National Geographic at 9 pm ET and available to stream on Disney+ and Hulu, the documentary takes viewers on an empathetic quest to understand how the line between “lover” and “fraud victim” gets blurred in romance scams that the Federal Trade Commission says cost Americans nearly $1.5 billion in losses each year.

title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘New York will explore other deals this weekend and Monday’
author: Antonio Losada
text:
No more fake basketball for the next eight months, folks!

The Knicks wrapped up the preseason with their most solid performance, defeated the Raps in New York, and will next see the banner(s) rise to the rafters of MSG.

Here’s the latest from everybody and their mothers.

On the Knicks’ progress over the past year heading into their title defense:

“I’m going to keep it real that there’s something in front of us. I’m not a fan of having an elephant in the room. I’ll address it: It’s about the process. It’s not about the end result. We can’t think about the end result right now. We have a ways to go. This is a new season, new team and we’re gonna have challenges in front of us.

“It’s like climbing a mountain. Sometimes you go a 100 yards, but you might get knocked back five yards. Hopefully, it’s not 50 yards, but you might get back five or 10 yards, and you regroup as a team, and you figure out how to keep going forward the right way.

“But making sure we embrace the process without slippage in that is going to be huge. And if I see us slipping up, it’s my job to let us know as a team that we’re off track. We need to get back on hopefully sooner than later.”

On why Jalen Brunson is the NBA’s best leader, as voted by GMs:

“He studies the game, and that helps a lot because you can always grow in any field you do. But he walks the talk. He works extremely hard, and he strives for perfection from himself. And when you do that, your peers see you do that, and you’re looked upon as the best player on the team, and it gives you credibility to tell somebody else when they’re not given their all or when they need to do this a little bit better or that a little bit better.”

On Brunson’s toughness and willingness to hold teammates accountable:

“He’s not afraid because, as a leader, sometimes you can be on an island because you have to always be conscious of ‘I got to do more, I got to do more’ in terms of work harder, focus, everybody’s going to make mistakes, but those little things. And so when you tell your teammates, they can get pissed at you, or they can be like, ‘hey, screw him because who is he to tell me what to do?’ And so you have to have some thick skin because it’s not going to always be you telling somebody to do something, then they embrace it. And I think Jalen has that thick skin and a toughness about him to be in a seat like this.”

On Brunson potentially becoming an NBA head coach after his playing career:

“I think Jalen has that thick skin and toughness about him to be in a seat like this. You won’t need to, though. My view? If you don’t want to… It’s up to you, Jalen.”

On what he expects from the Knicks’ final roster spot:

“If one of those guys makes our team, at least right now, they may not even play seven minutes — you know, seven straight minutes. And then at the end of the day, we just have to make a decision.”

On the mentality required from the Knicks’ third-string center:

“We just hope that there’s a passion and an energy and a focus coming from that spot because, I’m sure at times that person will start, at times they may be the first backup and at times they may be second backup. So as the minutes are fluctuating, you’re going to have to generate some internal energy at times, to go play in a low-minute game.

“Sometimes he’ll maybe not play one or two, maybe three games in a row. You look for that, and then you know, you just look for somebody that’s going to play hard at the end of the day – try to do the things that you’re asking on both sides of the floor. And bring a little something different than what the two guys in front of you bring.”

On Bruce Brown’s experience, toughness and versatility:

“Bruce has been through a lot with a lot of different teams at a pretty high level. His toughness, his experience, his feel, all those things — he’s a winner. It seems like every place he’s gone, he’s won, but all those things can add a lot to the program, and then he’s versatile both ends of the floor. He could play a few different positions offensively; he can guard a few different positions defensively. So a guy like that, especially a veteran winner, can be helpful to any team.”

On James Wiseman’s potential and development:

“He’s young, he’s talented, you know, he’s raw, still. I think he’s still trying to establish a foothold in this league. But with the God-given attributes he has, in terms of athleticism and length and quickness, [they] can bode well for him on both ends of the floor. And at 25 years old, he hasn’t even reached his prime, especially knowing he hadn’t played a ton of basketball; having a vertical threat at the rim will help [the Knicks], or could help everybody else play the game a little bit easier, whether it’s driving the basketball or playing pick and roll.”

On his recovery from wrist surgery:

“I had nine different casts. I was able to take it off if I ran or worked out with it. So I had one for workouts, one for showering and obviously one for everyday use.”

On maintaining the Knicks’ championship-winning approach entering a new season:

“I think what’s most important is that last year we took everything one day at a time. We were talking about — obviously, the topic was getting back to the conference finals and trying to advance. And I think for us now, the way we approached it last year was to take it one day at a time, every single day. So not talking about certain things.

“Obviously, we know what it takes, but just going into this with the same mindset for this journey. Even though it’s a new journey, it’s a different journey; the approach has to be the same, if not better.

“The first couple of weeks of the season is going to show us who we are and where we are. No matter what we’re doing, whether we’re playing great, playing bad, how are you going to be able to learn? And so, I mean, we’ll find a way. We’ll hold each other accountable, just like we did last year, and then we’ll be better.”

On the Knicks’ preseason progress and preparing to defend their championship:

“Each game got better and better. Just happy to be back. I feel like it’s a learning experience for us. We have to turn the page on last year and figure out how to get better every single day. It’s gonna be a different journey for us. Our mindset has to be different, and we’ll be ready to go.”

On the Knicks’ preseason finale and preparing for opening night:

“I thought today was a good dress rehearsal. It was cool, it was very nice to get back out there and get back into our flow and be really good. Obviously we have a lot of things to work on. But it was a good way to end the preseason.”

On how he feels physically and his rhythm entering the regular season:

“Yeah, I feel good. I feel really, really good.”

On who’s the biggest complainer to referees among Knicks:

“Josh Hart. Why’d y’all laugh? Did y’all agree with that or something? Everyone behind the camera, I just want y’all to know: y’all just clowned Josh Hart. That’s crazy for y’all to say — in New York, too.”

On choosing between winning another NBA championship and a World Series:

“Win a World Series, for sure. I already won an NBA championship.”

“Before the game starts, I always give everyone at the table, including the fans behind, a chance to really get into the game. Just giving everybody a fist bump down the line of the table, and then go on the court.”

On his favorite all-time big man:

“I think Hakeem. I feel like, in a way, he kind of is mythical, like Wilt Chamberlain… but I’ve been able to talk and meet Hakeem, and he’s an amazing, amazing human.”

On the Knicks’ roster decisions involving Bruce Brown, James Wiseman, Pacome Dadiet and Tyler Kolek:

“Brown and James Wiseman have made it through preseason cuts. The Knicks clearly like both players. But New York only has room under the second apron in team salary to keep one player. In order to keep both Brown and Wiseman, the Knicks would need to trade a player on a standard contract without taking back salary.

“My read heading into the weekend: Wiseman is a lock to make the roster. There is strong support to add Brown as well. The Knicks would need to make a trade by Monday afternoon if they want to keep Brown. I think they will explore all avenues to make that happen.

“It’s logical to assume that the Knicks will move third-year wing Pacome Dadiet. But I believe New York will explore other deals — including trades involving third-year guard Tyler Kolek — this weekend and Monday.

“The Knicks will be asking teams to take on a player without sending back salary. To get a deal done, New York may need to attach its own second-round picks (New York will have at least 11 second-round picks in the next seven drafts).”

On the Knicks’ handling of Karl-Anthony Towns’ contract negotiations:

“So, it was smart to dead the conversation. Now, how you deaded the conversation is the problem. I can’t find out on Twitter if that’s what happened…So if that’s the case (Towns learning from the media that the Knicks paused negotiations), then that’s a communication thing right there. [The Knicks] dropped the ball on that one for one. You don’t let that get outside. So again, I don’t know that. The only thing I’m saying is you don’t break up the family. That’s all I’m going to say. You don’t break up the family.”

On fulfilling his childhood dream of becoming a police officer:

“It’s something I always wanted to do since I was a kid. I remember back when I was in grade school, elementary school. They asked you on career day, ‘What do you want to be when you grow up?’ And my initial response was a police officer.”

On his family’s history in law enforcement:

“It runs in the family. My uncle was a captain. His brother was a deputy. My cousin is a captain. My sister’s in the academy. So, it’s a family tradition, basically.”

On the physical demands of police academy training compared with the NBA:

“Yeah, it was a little bit [more] challenging actually because now I’m running a lot more than I had before. Obviously, in the NBA you run short distances, right? And the police academy, you’re running more long-distance mileage.”

On his wife’s initial concerns about his decision to become a police officer:

“My wife at first was a little bit concerned because obviously being a police officer, there’s some danger to it. But if you are well-trained and you understand your policies and procedures, you’re able to somewhat have officer safety, which is very important, and that’s the goal.”

title: 'I am telling you the truth' - Carrick on Martinez fallout
text:
Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick says he is "telling the truth" when he says the club have moved on from Lisandro Martinez's explosive post-match comments this week.

Carrick's close friend and team-mate Wayne Rooney led the condemnation of Martinez, saying the Argentine defender could "rip the dressing room apart" with his attack on United's hierarchy after the 2-0 Champions League defeat by Atletico Madrid.

Former United skippers Roy Keane and Gary Neville have also had their say, among a huge amount of analysis.

Martinez has apologised for the timing of comments, which turned the spotlight on director of football Jason Wilcox, but not for the words themselves.

"There's a lot of people who say a lot of things - ex-pros or not ex-pros - it doesn't necessarily mean they understand what is going on here," said Carrick in his pre-match media conference at United's Carrington training ground.

"Just because people talk on the outside doesn't mean that is the truth. I am telling you the truth. The squad today was in a fantastic place, better than I have seen it for a while. That is it, plain and simple. We are living it every day and know what it feels like.

"We are emotional and care a lot. Sometimes someone says something that maybe you shouldn't say at that certain time, but it doesn't distract us from what we are creating here and the environment and spirit within the group.

"It [the squad] is not affected, I am telling you."

Carrick confirmed Martinez would be "part of the squad" for Sunday's Premier League trip to Leeds at Elland Road (14:00 BST).

Man Utd a circus after Martinez comments - Keane

Wilcox the target again in another damaging Man Utd fallout

Martinez singled out the 'technical director' for criticism in Madrid.

There was no mention of Wilcox in his statement, although the former Leeds and Blackburn player, who was made United's director of football in the aftermath of Dan Ashworth's sacking in December 2024, was part of the discussions with Martinez that led to his latest statement on his conduct.

Wilcox is back in the spotlight, after also being targeted by Ruben Amorim in his final press conference before his dismissal in January.

The 55-year-old has only spoken publicly once since, to United's own media channel, 12 months ago.

"I don't think it's for me to say whether he should or not," said Carrick, when asked if Wilcox should be the one explaining his actions to the media.

"I've got no problem sitting here, talking to you guys and leading the group, leading the team, leading the football club from this position. We're all in it together.

Carrick does not feel Martinez's failure to mention Wilcox by name is an issue.

"He's released his statement, he's realised he's made a mistake, and I think that's enough for all of us to move on with," he said.

"We ask for passion, we ask for emotion, we ask for fire and we ask for players to care. There's a way of doing that, and that's already been acknowledged.

"But we need to carry that intensity, that willingness, togetherness and spirit and everything else you can bring with that. As a group, we need to use it, and we've got to use it in the right way."

The negative headlines are the last thing Carrick needed at the present time.

His side go to Leeds on the back of a five-match winless run. United have not gone six games without a victory since the end of the 2018-19 campaign, just after Ole Gunnar Solskjaer had been confirmed as permanent manager.

Carrick knows the importance of ending that sequence in terms of easing the pressure on his own future.

However, he refuses to accept that as being crucial.

"I don't need results," he said. "We all need results.

"It's not about me. Manchester United is a lot bigger than any individual. It is bigger than me, bigger than any player, or anyone else who works at this football club. It always has been.

"I don't go into every day at work in this situation, [ahead of] this game, thinking it's about me. It's really not. It's about the football club; what we stand for, what we live for, the history, the things that we need to live up to. That's what drives us."

Martinez's outburst was triggered by United's lengthy injury list that led to Ayden Heaven playing at left-back in Madrid.

Cover for Luke Shaw, who missed the game through injury, and Benjamin Sesko were viewed by some as being crucial in the summer.

In addition to Shaw's absence, Sesko is yet to start a Premier League game this season.

The Slovenia forward, a £74m signing from RB Leipzig in August 2025, suffered a recurrence of the shin injury that curtailed his 2025-26 season in last month's EFL Cup defeat by Brighton.

For the third pre-match press conference running, Carrick said he was unable to give a timescale on Sesko's return.

"Ben's kind of still undergoing a couple of checks before we update on timelines," he said.

"We're just trying to be clear with what that looks like but he's still a little bit further away."

title: Which mountains will be on the 2027 Tour de France route? Pyrenees back to the fore, one ferociously difficult stage, and other emerging details
author: Alasdair Fotheringham
text:
The 2027 Tour de France looks set to have its major mountain showdown in the Pyrenees next year, with a summit finish on the notoriously difficult Col du Portet a frontrunner to finish off what could well be the toughest single climbing stage of the race.

Described back in 2021 by Tadej Pogačar as a "never-ending story," according to La Nouvelle République des Pyrénées, this time round the Col du Portet could be preceded by two historically famous Hors Catégorie ascents, the Tourmalet and Aubisque, making for a ferociously difficult stage.

2027's Tour is widely reported to see the Pyrenees taking over from the Alps in 2026 as the scenario for next July's main climbing challenges, with stages 18 and 19 likely the key dates in the country's southernmost mountain range.

Other rumours about the major peaks of the 2027 race include an ascent of the Jura's highest paved mountain pass, Le Grand Colombier, as the curtain-raiser to the Tour's climbing stages at the end of the first week.

However, as the date of the route publication on Thursday October 22 in Paris looms fast on the horizon, the most striking mountain rumours are the possible inclusion of the Col du Portet. Less famous than the Tourmalet or Aubisque, but also ranked Hors Categorie, the Portet's viciously irregular slopes first appeared in the 2018 Tour. That year it was the finish of one of the Tour's shortest-ever mountain stages - just 65km long - that saw Nairo Quintana take his last ever victory in the race.

The Tour then returned to Col du Portet in 2021, when the top favourite both now and then, Tadej Pogačar (UAE Team Emirates-XRG), won the stage ahead of Jonas Vingegaard (Visma-Lease a Bike) and simultaneously further cemented his considerable overall lead. With Pogačar very likely looking to fight for a record-equalling sixth Tour in 2027, the odds of a repeat battle next summer with the Dane on the same 16.2-kilometre ascent, with many segments at over 9%, are not small.

Although the date for the possible ascent of Col du Portet is provisionally said to be stage 18, another day's racing is also expected in the Pyrenees 24 hours later.

But in stark contrast to stage 18, no information has yet been leaked regarding potential climbs for stage 19. However, it would seem likely that the stage takes place at the western end of the mountain range, prior to the final weekend's return to Paris.

Overall, as reported by , the specialist website in Tour de France pre-route publication news, the first week of the race looks much easier than in 2026. This July saw the Pyrenees feature, albeit briefly, as soon as stage 3, then again in a much fuller format across the Tourmalet to Gavarnie-Gèdre on stage 6.

Next summer after the transfer from Cardiff following three stages in Britain and a long hike across northern France, the first summit finish could be on stage 9 at Le Grand Colombier. Another very irregular climb with stretches at 20% in places, the last ascent of the HC climb in the Jura in 2023 saw Vingegaard and Pogačar maintain their stalemate at the top of GC.

There were seven stages in the Alps in 2026, and far fewer are expected in 2027, but the few opportunities there will likely be memorable ones all the same. After a rest day in the northern Alps, racing is expected to resume on stage 10 with a visit to the famous World Championships circuit in Sallanches.

The circuit's principal challenge, the Côte de Domancy, is both where Hinault took one of the toughest ever Worlds in 1980, and also a preview for the World Championships of 2027, with two highlights being the elite men's road race taking place on the same course next August 28 and the equivalent women's event a week later.

Major Alpine finishes are expected on stage 11 and possibly stage 12, with Le Dauphiné Libéré reporting that the first day could see a finish at the Col de Samoëns 1600. Part of the same Grand Massif range which contains the much better-known Col de Joux Plane, the Samoëns climb is a relatively benign 11 kilometres long, and its 900 metres of climbing are relatively steady.

The same goes for the next day's predicted big final climb, Col des Saisies, 14.6km or 15.2km long depending on the approach road, but with a gradient never reaching more than 8%.

Often used in early parts of the Alpine stages – like in 2023 when the race ended by crossing the much more difficult Col de la Loze – 2027 could be the first ever summit finish on the Saisies. However, its easier slopes once again will ensure the Pyrenees remain the crunch stages of the race.

Before the Tour gets there, though, there'll be time for a very difficult stage across the Massif Central, featuring 4,500 metres of vertical climbing, according to and . It is said to finish at the airfield in Mende, which has been the scene of some memorable victories by versatile breakaway specialists like Steve Cummings and Michael Matthews in recent years .

But Mende's most memorable day in the GC of the Tour remains 1995 when Laurent Jalabert and the ONCE team all but toppled Miguel Indurain en route to his record-equalling fifth overall win. 32 years later, it remains to be seen if Tadej Pogačar is by then en route to an all-time sixth success, and if anybody is in a position to stop him.

title: Track World Championships: Great Britain adds two more gold medals on Day 3
author: Owen Rogers
text:
Great Britain continued their successful run on day three of the UCI Track World Championships, taking home more silverware, with Mark Stewart winning the men’s Points Race title and Anna Morris taking the women’s Omnium title in the Shanghai championships.

In the other events, Jeffrey Hoogland took a fifth rainbow jersey in the men’s kilometre time trial, while Jonathan Milan backed up the Individual Pursuit world record he set in the semi-finals with a rainbow jersey.

With three of the five days complete, Great Britain top the medal table, adding a silver and a bronze medal to their tally, Emma Finucane taking second in the Women’s Sprint and Joseph Truman taking third place behind Hoogland in the Kilo.

Great Britain’s Mark Stewart won a brilliantly entertaining Points Race, beating the 2021 rainbow jersey into second place with a powerful and clever ride. Portugal’s Carlos Salgueiro was third.

The race finished in dramatic style with Carl-Frederik Bévort only just failing to take a lap, which would have seen the Danish rider take the win. In the end he won the final sprint, but was just off the back of the bunch and took fourth place.

Held over 160 laps of the Shanghai track, the 40km race began in restrained style, Red Walters (Grenada) and Ni Li (China) winning the opening sprints, though as the race developed Australian Liam Walsh moved into the lead, taking a lap around a third of the way into the race. However, by the time he reached the back of the bunch, the peloton was in tatters, and he was unable to consolidate, eventually losing that advantage and the 20 points that went with it.

Thomas was particularly aggressive, though Stewart was stealthily picking up points behind him, and the pair traded punches all race long, while Salgueiro was closing in. The race swung Stewart’s way with 30 laps to go, the British rider winning five points, while Thomas failed to score.

After a first attack from Dévort attack was brought back Salgueiro moved to within four points of Stewart with 20 laps to go and closer still 10 laps later. However, Bévort’s last gasp attempt worked in the Briton’s favour, and he took a career first rainbow jersey.

Anna Morris took Great Britain’s second gold medal of the day, winning the Women’s Omnium, taking her first bunch race rainbow jersey after successes in the Team and Individual Pursuits.

Morris rode strongly and intelligently throughout the four race event, finishing the top three of the first three events then defending brilliantly in the fourth. In the end she scored 125 points, beating Tsuyaka Uchino (Japan) and Amalie Dideriksen (Denmark), who was third.

Morris moved into the overall lead in event two, the Tempo, while behind her Lotte Kopecky (Belgium) moved up the overall standings, taking second place, with French woman Victoire Berteau in third place.

Morris remained attentive throughout the Elimination race, riding aggressively and often on the front, but was the last rider eliminated, with Berteau taking the sprint ahead of recently crowned Elimination World Champion Kopecky.

With all the points scored in the Points Race counting towards the total, the final event was hugely important, and Morris started well, taking a maximum five points in the opening sprint with 70 of the 80 laps remaining. Milan was flying from the first lap, riding one second per kilometre faster than his rival and apparently chasing a second record time.
