title: Revealed: VW, Ford and Tesla batteries linked to destructive deforestation of indigenous lands
author: Stefano Valentino in Sulawesi and Ajit Niranjan
text:
Mines in supply chains of western carmakers linked to widespread deforestation of primary rainforest in nickel-rich lands inhabited by Tolaki people in Indonesia

V olkswagen, Ford and Tesla are among the electric carmakers whose batteries may contain nickel mined in indigenous woodlands plagued by deforestation, an analysis has found, highlighting the struggle to make vehicles that are free from environmental destruction.

Corporate disclosures and trade flows from the last two years show mines in the battery supply chains of automotive giants are linked to the loss of trees in Sulawesi, a wildlife hotspot in Indonesia that houses the world’s largest nickel deposits. The metal is widely used in cathodes in car batteries because it boosts energy density and increases range.

Ore from the Cahaya and Hengjaya mines was traced through regional smelters and Chinese processing plants run by Zhejiang Huayou Cobalt, a cathode manufacturer that supplies CATL, the world’s largest battery maker. Huayou’s corporate reports list US and European carmakers as end-users, while additional corporate files and trade data show a separate route from Huayou to LG, a South Korean group that also supplies battery products to leading carmakers, via Poland.

Satellite analysis shows the mines have led to widespread deforestation of primary rainforest in nickel-rich lands inhabited by the indigenous Tolaki people.

“We used to ask the forest for protection in return for our offerings,” said Wadimula, a Tolaki elder whose home sits on the edge of the 21,000-hectare Cahaya mining concession. “Destroying it means destroying our own life.”

Electric vehicles are less environmentally harmful than fossil fuel-burning engines, which spew gases that foul the air and heat the planet, but western carmakers have struggled to clean up supply chains for batteries built with critical minerals from Africa, Asia and South America. Environmental groups warn that a failure to curb the boom of material-hungry SUVs is exacerbating the destruction by increasing the quantity mined.

Ore from the two mining concessions is sent to a nickel smelter in an industrial complex in Morowali, on Indonesia’s eastern coast, operated by Huayou’s local subsidiary, where limonite is refined into mixed hydroxide precipitate, the primary raw material used to make battery cathodes.

In 2024, $606m worth of mixed hydroxide precipitate was shipped from the Morowali plant to ports in China, followed by further shipments worth $470m in 2025. The processed ore was transported overland to Huayou cathode manufacturing sites in Quzhou, near Shanghai, and Yulin, near the border with Vietnam.

Public filings do not disclose specific volumes or timings of sales from Huayou to CATL, which would be needed to directly connect specific ore shipments to car batteries, but Huayou confirmed group-level supplies to CATL in response to a regulatory inquiry by the Shanghai Stock Exchange in 2024. Chengdu B&M, a downstream subsidiary of Huayou, has also confirmed the supply of “large quantities” to CATL.

The investigation, published in partnership with Voxeurop and other European media partners, traced shipments from mines and refineries in Sulawesi to China, and then again from Huayou cathode and CATL battery factories to the assembly lines of carmakers in the US and Europe. Volkswagen’s facility in Braunschweig, for instance, received a shipment in October 2024 of 24 tonnes of cell modules worth about $390,000, according to data from Volza, a trade platform.

The shift to a carbon-free economy is pushing up demand for critical minerals in countries with weak environmental safeguards, though experts have argued the mining boom can be tempered without slowing the shift away from dirty fuels. In 2023, a report found lithium demand in the US transport sector could be reduced by 18% to 66% compared with a business-as-usual scenario, by improving public transport, walking and cycling more, and buying smaller cars. Better recycling could bring demand reductions as high as 92%, the report found.

Global demand for nickel is set to double to 5.5m tonnes by 2040, according to the International Energy Agency, much of it mined in Indonesia and then refined in China. The loss of trees in mining concessions means the carbon footprint of nickel from the worst mines may be up to 500 times greater than previously reported, a study in Nature Communications found last year.

The Cahaya and Hengjaya mines are located in woodlands designated as “production forest”, which are intended for forestry rather than industrial activities. However, successive Indonesian governments have weakened safeguards and carved out exemptions for miners as demand for nickel has soared.

Nickel mining may be responsible for two-thirds of the forest loss recorded since 2001 within the area encompassed by the Cahaya concession, and over half of the loss in the Hengjaya concession, spatial analysis conducted by geospatial firm The TreeMap suggests.

Sulawesi Cahaya Mineral (SCM), the company that operates the Cahaya mine, contributed to clearing an additional 330 hectares of forest in 2024, according to an analysis by Auriga, an Indonesian nonprofit. The same year, it delivered 11m tonnes of limonite ore – almost all of its production – to Huayou’s smelter. Deliveries increased to nearly 12.5m tonnes throughout 2025. The plant also continued to receive ore from the Hengjaya mine by road, local lorry drivers said.

SCM received two administrative sanctions last year for illegally clearing more than 450 hectares of forest beyond the boundaries of its permitted clearing area. The company is a subsidiary of Merdeka Battery Materials, part of a group whose shareholders include Huayou and CATL.

The carmakers identified as end-users of Huayou cathodes or recipients of shipments from CATL include Volkswagen, Volvo, Ford , General Motors, Tesla, BMW, Stellantis and Hyundai. Mercedes-Benz was separately linked to Huayou.…

title: From Dallaglio’s medals to Cantona’s shorts, sporting memorabilia is big business | Emma John
author: Emma John
text:
Like transfer fees and ticket prices, mementoes are one more marker of sport’s rampant self-inflation

T he auctioneer cradled his gavel in his palm like a pipe, the handle pointing towards him. It gave his patter the air of a Victorian gentleman holding forth by the mantelpiece in a period drama. “Are you bidding, Wilf? You’re waving at me.” Under the hammer was a Barclays Manager of the Month trophy, complete with travel case, but no indication of which Premier League luminary once owned it. It outstripped its estimate and sold for £700.

An hour and a half into what Budds auction house dubbed its “Octoberfest” of sporting memorabilia, David Convery at the podium showed no sign of fatigue, save the occasional swig from a water bottle. There were 332 lots in total; Convery regularly manages sales with twice as many. In his three decades as an auctioneer he’s even secured some world-record prices, from the oldest surviving FA Cup to Pelé’s 1970 World Cup final shirt.

But sporting collectibles have never been bigger business than now. This week a jersey worn by Michael Jordan in the second game of the 1998 NBA finals – his “Last Dance” season for the Chicago Bulls – sold for over £10m , the kind of sum that might otherwise buy you a Mayfair townhouse. It was unprecedented in basketball but only just – two weeks previously, the jersey Jordan wore in game three had gone for £9.3m. And that had broken the record set by – you better believe it – Jordan’s game one jersey, which Sotheby’s sold in 2022.

Last week’s Budds catalogue was never going to reach those heights but it still contained some star items. Almost all were the property of Lawrence Dallaglio, the former England rugby union captain, declared bankrupt a year ago and now treading the well-worn path of sportspeople forced to sell their mementoes of the glory days. Seven years ago Boris Becker raised nearly £700,000 by selling trophies he had amassed, including a replica of the US Open trophy he won against Ivan Lendl in 1989. Unfortunately in his case it wasn’t enough to prevent further trouble with the taxman.

Running an auction is like writing a set list – you can’t just start with your biggest numbers, you have to warm up the audience, build to the good stuff. Diane Modahl’s leotard from the 1998 Commonwealth Games proved, somewhat ironically, a false start; no takers, even at £50 and with the 800m runner’s spikes and signature thrown in. A £5 note autographed by Jack Nicklaus did considerably better, and gradually the ephemera – signed prints, photos and programmes – gave way to more substantial stuff, like cricket caps and blazers from the days when England still wore the MCC’s colours and crest overseas.

Admittedly, those postwar names are out of vogue now: still, it was a surprise to discover you could pick up one of Trevor Bailey’s touring blazers for less than you’d pay for a decent new one at John Lewis. Or that Paul Stirling’s Ireland T20 shirt is worth more than a pair of Godfrey Evans’s wicketkeeping gloves.

Dallaglio’s collection, when it arrived, was one for the bigger spenders. A set of tankards sold for £1,600 – perhaps to a rugby fan who knows he can never emulate the former England captain on the pitch but likes the idea of matching him at the bar. His 2003 World Cup winner’s medal was the prize item. It went for £54,000, near the bottom of its estimate, yet even more poignant was the rapacious flurry of bids on his England and Lions caps, with their old-fashioned gold braid and tassel, and individual numbers stitched on the peak. As Convery himself said, it’s rare for such items to make it to market.

Still, no time for sentiment at an auction. The lots marched on, relentlessly, from the sublime to the ridiculous: Harry Kane shirts, Eric Cantona’s shorts, and the coffee table Des Lynam presided over in the BBC television studio at the 1998 Fifa World Cup. Whether Robbie Williams, its previous owner, was a careful one was not disclosed, but the added stardust fuelled a transatlantic contest between the UK and the US, with Blighty ultimately triumphing for £800.

The US has always valued both on- and off-field artefacts – witness its trading card tradition, or the brawls in the bleachers when a baseball is hit straight into the stands. The jersey that Babe Ruth wore when he hit his “called shot” against the Chicago Cubs in the 1932 World Series – arguably the most legendary moment in his storied career – remains the most expensive item of sports memorabilia ever, having sold for over £18m in 2024 . But globalisation – and, needless to say, the internet – has transformed the market in the past two decades.

Nowhere is that better seen than the price surge in game-worn soccer shirts: the most iconic are now bought by billionaires with the same eye for appreciation as for a Picasso or a Van Gogh. The aerial backpass that enabled Diego Maradona’s Hand of God goal may have been Steve Hodge’s nadir in an England shirt, but swapping that shirt for Maradona’s No 10 when the final whistle blew was a brilliant midfield manoeuvre. Four years ago, an anonymous buyer paid over £7m for it . Six of Lionel Messi’s Argentina shirts, meanwhile, recently proved to be worth more than the entire turnover of his own clothing line.

Perhaps – like transfer fees and ticket prices – this is just one more marker of sport’s rampant self-inflation. Its move from the immeasurable, nonsensical passions of traditional fandom to the hard metallic truths of the trading floor. After three hours, the auctioneer was still going strong, his mesmeric rat-a-tat punctuated by the soft digital ding every time the website registered a sale. And I was as helplessly hooked as a TikTok-scrolling teenager.

title: The right’s scrounger rhetoric dominates the benefits debate. Labour must fight back – and win | Frances Ryan
author: Frances Ryan
text:
The prime minister has a once-in-a-generation chance to reintroduce fairness to the system. He has to seize the moment

B ack in 2009, months before the coalition government unleashed sweeping austerity, the then Conservative backbencher Iain Duncan Smith produced a study that would go on to lay the foundations for the rollout of universal credit. Now, nearly two decades later, Duncan Smith and his thinktank, the Centre for Social Justice (CSJ), has published State of Dependency: a landmark report promising to expose “the full scale of Britain’s worklessness crisis”.

The study paints a picture of mass benefits reliance: it identifies 3,400 local areas where more than half the working-age population are on out-of-work benefits, or “economic opiates”, as the authors call them. They’ve even provided an interactive map (in the yellow and black colours of a road hazard sign, no less) so members of the public can type in their postcode to see if their neighbourhood is “a welfare hotspot”.

This is not just another ugly social policy report from a politically sidelined former minister – it is a gauntlet being thrown down ahead of Britain’s big benefits debate.

Next month, the government is expected to release two major reports into the social safety net: the Timms review on personal independence payments (Pip), which pays for some of the extra costs of disability in England and Wales, and the Milburn review into young people who are out of work.

It wouldn’t be overstating the importance of Westminster reviews to say their recommendations could shape the future of our welfare state for decades to come. With almost 1 million young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) and the disability benefits bill rising in cash terms, Andy Burnham will face immense pressure to use the proposals to launch a once-in-a-generation overhaul of the social security system.

An overhaul in itself is no bad thing. Disabled people applying for benefits face a debilitating mess of bureaucracy and barriers, while too many young people have been abandoned, facing greater obstacles and fewer services. The question is, will the overhaul actually improve conditions for the people who rely on it, or buckle to the anti-benefit sentiment that’s been bubbling up for months?

That the right is not currently in power won’t stop it from wielding significant influence on what’s to come, in large part thanks to its dominance of Britain’s media ecosystem. Legacy media are not even hiding their attempts to shape November’s reforms before they are announced, with the Times this week launching a “ welfare inquiry ” to investigate the impact of the benefits “crisis” on public finances.

Some of this is made up of concrete policy proposals, such as the Daily Mail’s pitch to radically means-test Pip . But increasingly much of it is just vibes, a vague sense that this disability problem is getting out of control (or having one is becoming “cool” , as the Telegraph recently put it), and that disabled people – particularly the young – are somehow grifting “perks” while everyone else struggles with rising bills.

The changes in how people consume media since the last major benefits reforms in the early 2010s mean the risks of misinformation and outright bigotry are even greater. Last week, Nigel Farage announced plans for a new video studio in Westminster for the launch of Reform TV on YouTube , with the party’s proposed £50bn benefits cuts presumably being lined up as viral content.

Keep an eye out too for a revival of the striver v scrounger rhetoric as energy and housing costs are set to lead to the worst living standards in modern times by 2029-30. There are few easier ways to convince workers that the unemployed should go hungry than when they’re cutting back on their own food shop. It is telling that the CSJ study includes a section directly comparing “economically inactive claimants” with workers: someone on minimum wage would have to work six days a week to match “the security, cash and ease” a disabled person gets from a package of state benefits, it proclaims. About 1.4 million foreign nationals receive working-age benefits, it ominously adds. Divide and conquer never gets old.

A Labour government is no guarantee these divisions – worker v claimants, old v young, migrant v citizen – won’t be espoused from the cabinet table. No recommendations by Timms or Milburn have been confirmed yet, but Whitehall sources say there are potential plans to scrap a key part of universal credit for under-25s and replace it with a multi-billion pound package to get people back into work.

Sure, it’s depressing if ministers are tempted to bow to the prevailing political winds by pulling cash from young people, but it’s not exactly surprising. For decades, the right has set the boundaries for what Britain’s safety net can be, resulting in little more than subsistence-level benefit rates, an ever crueller culture of testing and a sicker population.

The conventional wisdom has always been that change can only go one way: the benefits system can repeatedly become more punitive and error-strewn, but never more compassionate or accurate. For a leader who has defined himself as someone unafraid of large-scale change, Burnham is well placed to challenge that orthodoxy – if he wants. The opportunity to transform the benefits system does not come up often, and it is rarer still for a Conservative prime minister not to be at the helm.…

title: Commercial kitchen staff exposed to high levels of air pollution, study finds
author: Gary Fuller
text:
US research says nitrogen dioxide in restaurants that cook with gas can exceed WHO limits, which also affects diners

E ach time we enjoy a meal out or order a takeaway, someone cooks for us in a commercial kitchen. In the UK, 3.6 million people work in catering and hospitality. In the US it is estimated at close to 16 million . A first-of-its-kind study in the US has found catering staff can experience high air pollution at work – and that this can affect diners too.

Dr Drew Michanowicz, senior author of the study at non-profit research institute PSE Healthy Energy , said: “I was motivated by what we have learned over the years about what just 30 minutes of gas cooking can do to air quality in homes with the realisation that millions of people cook for a living for hours on end.”

The researchers measured air pollution in 27 kitchens including fine-dining and casual full-service restaurants, those serving pizza and Chinese cuisine, catering facilities and kitchens in senior-living communities, universities and schools.

Although the kitchens met US legal limits for air pollution in workplaces, nitrogen dioxide in 17 kitchens was greater than the World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines for indoor air . All of these kitchens cooked with fossil-gas or propane.

Nitrogen dioxide is a pollutant in diesel exhaust, which has led to many UK and European cities introducing clean air and low-emission zones .

Three all-electric kitchens, a full-service restaurant, a school cafeteria, and a conference centre kitchen were part of the study. These had the lowest air pollution, indicating benefits from decarbonisation in catering and ending fossil-gas combustion.

The electric kitchens also had the lowest temperatures, an obvious benefit for staff welfare.

This summer’s European heatwave forced some restaurants in the UK to cut hours or close due sweltering conditions. Christopher Galarza , a chef who worked with the researchers, said: “I’ve worked in kitchens where the heat was so intense that you would finish a shift drenched in sweat, dehydrated and physically spent.”

The study also found air pollution did not stay in the kitchen. Median concentrations in dining areas were greater than WHO guidelines for outdoor air pollution .

Dr Yannai Kashtan, first author of the study from PSE Heathy Energy, said: “It is difficult to contextualise the relative risk to diners, but as a diner in a restaurant with gas-fired appliances you may be exposed to elevated levels of nitrogen dioxide.”

One result surprised the research team. Kashtan said: “In two-thirds of the gas kitchens, we measured higher levels of pollution overnight and in the early morning, when all the appliances were off. The culprit? Pilot lights that burn 24/7, whether or not ventilation is on.”

In the UK many commercial kitchens have automatic systems that cut off gas when ventilation is not operating.

Michanowicz said commercial-grade cooking appliances were not included in US energy efficiency regulations that led to pilot lights being phased out in the residential sector. “In most full-service kitchens with multiple appliances like ranges, griddles, fryers, ovens, steamers, and broilers, upwards of 20-30 small flames may be constantly burning,” said Michanowicz.

In the study, air pollution from pilot lights spread into dining areas, increasing exposure for cleaners and other workers and the health risk for other people in multi-use buildings.

title: Ship attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports slow
text:
The number of ships that have reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz has hit a record high, BBC Verify analysis of data from a UK maritime agency shows.

Twelve vessels were attacked between 5 and 11 October - the largest number of weekly strikes reported to the UK's Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency since the US-Israeli war with Iran began. The previous week saw 10 ships reporting attacks.

Six of the vessels were struck last Sunday, according to the UKMTO - a one-day high. So far this week, there have been four reported attacks.

As the number of strikes has risen, the recovery in oil shipments through the strait seen last month has slowed, industry data suggests.

BBC Verify collated incident reports published by the UKMTO on its website and created a timeline based on the first date cited in each report. This is approximate because some incidents use the date of the attack and some the date on which it was reported.

Experts say Tehran has been attacking ships in an effort to assert greater control over the waterway as the US military has increased the number of tankers it is shepherding through the south of the strait to evade Iranian strikes.

Iran is also carrying out more attacks on vessels further away from the Strait of Hormuz, according to experts.

The US military's Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, posted on social media that despite the attacks "commercial traffic continues to flow through the Strait of Hormuz with co-ordinated protection from US forces and regional partners".

The aftermath of one of Sunday's six reported attacks was captured in verified footage showing the Nicaragua-flagged tanker Petro Dolphin on fire, as filmed by the crew on a smaller boat nearby.

The vessel was struck by a drone close to the Sohar Anchorage, Oman, more than 250km (150 miles) from the strait, according to the maritime intelligence firm Vanguard.

Eleven Indian seafarers were rescued but two are still missing, the Forward Seamen's Union of India said.

Attacks have continued this week with the container ship GFS Pride sinking after a strike by an unknown projectile in the strait on Tuesday. Twenty-one crew were safely evacuated.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) published footage of what appeared to be the same ship sinking. It said the vessel was carrying "2,500 containers of contraband" and had taken an "unauthorised route".

Middle East oil exports have slowed as the number of ship strikes has risen.

About 12.6 million barrels per day went through the strait on 13 October, below the 15 million reported at the end of September, data from trade intelligence firm Kpler shows. This compares with a pre-war baseline of some 17 million barrels per day.

The recent increase in attacks comes as US Navy data indicates the number of vessels given assistance to navigate the Strait of Hormuz during the first 10 days of October was up 85% compared with the same period in August.

Most of the oil being shipped from Gulf Arab states recently has been carried using a "shuttle" system where a fleet of tankers load up and sail through the strait before transferring their cargo to larger tankers in the Gulf of Oman.

These shuttle ships use a route close to Oman's coastline. Iran says this is "unauthorised" and insist vessels take an alternative route closer to its own shore.

So-called assisted transits were a key factor in helping drive oil flows from the Middle East back towards pre-war levels in September. This does not include Iranian exports which have completely stalled as a result of the US blockade of Iranian ports and ships.

Martin Kelly, CEO of Orbital Risk Intelligence, said Iran has "evolved its strategy" in response to this loosening of its control over the strait and has been carrying out "near daily or multiple attacks every single day".

"The aim here is to stop the ships going through and to deter others," he added.

The IRGC's navy has said strikes would not be "limited to the Strait of Hormuz" and later announced a "new deployment formation" across the region, according to state media.

Martin Kelly told BBC Verify that Iran is widening its attacks and targeting ships near the coast of Gulf Arab states and in the Gulf of Oman.

A tanker was struck by multiple projectiles north of Qatar on Thursday 8 October, more than 500km (310 miles) from the strait, resulting in multiple reported casualties, according to Vanguard.

Another tanker was attacked close to the UAE town of Al-Jazirah al-Hamra on Friday 9 October, Vanguard said.

Verified footage shows crew members running across the deck and putting on lifejackets as a large cloud of black smoke rises over the ship.

title: Knicks 122, Raptors 120: Scenes from Towns toppling Toronto
author: Russell Richardson
text:
Tonight at Madison Square Garden, the Knicks played their final preseason game—a rematch with a Toronto team that clobbered the reserves on Tuesday. This time, the fight was fairer. The visitors played their starters (Immanuel Quickley, RJ Barrett, Scottie Barnes, Kawhi Leonard, and Jakob Poeltl), but so did the Knicks (mostly: Mohamed Diawara took Josh Hart’s spot). Determined to not lay a complete goose egg this preseason, coach Mike Brown returned to his starters in the fourth quarter, and that gave them just enough juice to win, 122-120.

The game started on the right foot. Resuming their championship ways, Karl-Anthony Towns took turns with Jalen Brunson on give-and-go sequences that were money in the bank. When KAT sat around the three-minute mark, he had five points, five boards, and six dimes on perfect shooting. Included in those buckets was a laser from deep. Every time he swishes the net this season will sound like a whispered, “Pay the man.”

Across the aisle, Barnes converted his first four shots for an early nine points. That’s what has Toronto fans excited: four scoring options in their starting lineup to complement a top-ten defense. Neither team lived up to their defensive potential in the first frame, however. They allowed each other to shoot over 60% from all areas of the floor by the midway mark.

Even Diawara (carrying two fouls) laced a corner three. Not to be outdone, Miles McBride (who had two triples through four preseason games) dropped three threes in his first four minutes. Those were positives. What wasn’t: Pacome Dadiet checking in and promptly getting stripped while over-dribbling. Soon after, he flushed a pass from Brunson, but there was nothing to change our minds about the youngster. In preseason form, the two teams traded buckets, but by the quarter’s end, the good guys were up, 35-32.

Andre Drummond provided a steady hand off the bench, hoovering up rebounds (seven in seven minutes), rattling in a jump hook, tipping in a putback, and making a free throw or two. That softened the sting of seeing Mitchell Robinson doing his best Bill Russell impersonation at TD Garden. Also off the bench, Landry Shamet picked Jamal Shead’s pocket and, on a fast break, fed the trailing Jordan Clarkson. Just a few pros giving the team solid minutes.

Toronto fell behind by 10, but clawed their way back by disrupting New York’s offense. Shead and Jamison Battle hit threes; the former is a defensive pest and blocked two perimeter shots (Diawara, Shamet), while Collin Murray-Boyles intercepted two Brunson passes. Towns had lost the touch, missing two threes and coughing up the rock twice. Nonetheless, New York won the quarter 28–26, and entered intermission ahead, 63-58.

The hosts had shot 55% overall, 47% from deep, and had a 32-18 advantage in the paint. They’d out-bounded the Raps, 26-16, but turned the ball over 12 times, which kept them from running up the score. Top scorers through the half were Barnes (15 points) and Mikal Bridges (14 points, two blocks, 6-of-8 shooting). Bridges made all five of his two-point attempts and canned a Brunson-assisted three, but his jump-out-of-the-seat play was the block of Barrett’s three at the buzzer. I’d say Mikal is ready for opening night.

With our team fumbling and bumbling after the break, the guests gained ground and overran the score, 69-66, with scores from Leonard, Quickley, Barrett, and Murray-Boyles. For the Knicks, Anunoby continued to struggle from yard, having made just 1-of-11 through the preason after his miss early in the third. Diawara committed another foul trying to grab a board, and his fourth infraction in 13 minutes earned him a quick hook.

Remember when Brunson joked that his SNL episode would be like a Knicks playoff game: crappy through three quarters with a big finish at the end? The Knicks still feel like a team that can’t play a complete game. We cheered when Towns dished to a cutting Shamet for a dunk (yes, Shamet!), but no one boxed out Barrett at the other end for an easy response.

Coach Mike Brown wanted this win, we gather, as he left Brunson and Towns on the floor late in the third quarter. Brunson steadied the offense, scoring seven points and dishing two dimes to fuel a 9–0 run. Dadiet made a hook to tie it at 74 (then missed a dunk), and KAT connected from deep to regain the lead. With a 19-5 run—including OG’s first basket after missing seven shots—our heroes finished the frame up, 87-79.

A few times tonight, we saw Jose Alvarado and Drummond playing a nice two-man game. When Andre drove to the cup for a finger-roll, it gave the home team double-digit lead. Alvarado made his first three dingers from deep, too. We’re eager to see more of this dynamic duo. The Dinos went on a Barnes-heavy run and scored eight unanswered to tie the game around the 9:30 mark, but then Alvarado, Anunoby, and Shamet stimulated a seven-point swing to stop the insanity.

The toughest move of the night was Mike Brown refusing to go winless this preseason. At 8:28, he subbed Brunson, Towns, and Diawara in to hold the lead alongside Shamet and Anunoby. OAKAAKUYOAKs Barrett and Quickley would not willingly roll over on their old home court, however, scoring their 21st and 18th points respectively. For a scrimmage, this one was competitive late.

When Towns sat at 5:15, his box score read 13 points, 15 boards, and nine assists and his team clung to a six-point advantage. It would be up to the reserves to close out the dub: Tyler Kolek, Tyler Nickel, Dadiet, Diawara, and James Wiseman.

Tonight we got just four minutes of Wiseman, who seems to have secured the third-string center spot with today’s annoucement that Drew Eubanks has a torn pectoral.

With a minute to go, Jaden Bradley had tied the score at 117. From there, though, the Tylers combined for five points (including a trey for Kolek) that offset a late bucket by Malachi Smith. These games don’t count, but this one sure had some fun moments.

Opening night is Tuesday, with a banner and the Sixers. Rest up, Knickerbockers.
